## Project Proposal/Statistical Analysis Plan

Link to your team's Github Repo: <https://github.com/ZhihaoZhou0/IDS702-Statistics-Project>

### Dataset Option 1

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Project Title: Sleep Duration and Body Mass Index Among U.S. Adults: Does the Association Differ by Gender?

Data citation:

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Health Statistics. (2009--2012). *National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), 2009--2010 and 2011--2012* \[Data set\]. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/

Pruim, R. (2015). *NHANES: Data from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Study* (Version 2.1.0) \[R package\]. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.NHANES

Original data collection date: Survey data were collected in the 2009--2010 and 2011--2012 NHANES cycles; the curated R package (version 2.1.0) was published on July 2, 2015.

Data pull date: October 29, 2026

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1 Research Question

**Primary RQ:** Among U.S. adults, is nightly sleep duration associated with body mass index (BMI) after adjusting for age, physical activity, income-to-poverty ratio, race/ethnicity, education, and smoking history, and does this association differ between men and women?

**Backup RQ:** Among U.S. adults, is BMI associated with the odds of having been diagnosed with diabetes after adjusting for age, race/ethnicity, income-to-poverty ratio, education, smoking history, and physical activity, and does this association differ between men and women?

#### 2 Study Population

The observation unit is an individual adult participant in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). NHANES is conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) at the CDC and uses a complex, stratified, multistage probability design to sample the non-institutionalized civilian U.S. population. Participants complete an in-home interview (demographic, socioeconomic, and health-behavior questions) and a standardized physical examination in a mobile examination center, where measurements such as height, weight, and blood pressure are taken.

We use the `NHANES` R package, which contains 10,000 observations resampled from the 2009--2010 and 2011--2012 cycles using the survey weights, so that the data approximate a simple random sample of the U.S. population. Because of this resampling, some participants appear more than once; we will keep one record per participant ID. Several variables of interest (e.g., education, smoking history) were only collected for participants aged 20 and older, so we restrict the analysis to adults aged 20+. After removing duplicate records and restricting to adults, the analytic sample contains 4,654 participants. Missingness among the variables of interest is low (the largest is the poverty ratio, with 366 missing values, about 8%), so we plan a complete-case analysis.

#### 3 Outcomes, Exposures, and Additional Variables of Interest

3.1 Primary Outcome(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| BMI | Body mass index, calculated from measured weight and height | Continuous, kg/m² |
| Diabetes *(backup RQ)* | Whether the participant has been told by a doctor or health professional that they have diabetes | Factor: No, Yes |

3.2 Primary Independent Variable(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| SleepHrsNight | Self-reported number of hours of sleep usually obtained on weeknights or workdays | Integer, hours |
| Gender | Gender of the participant (effect modifier; interaction with sleep duration) | Factor: female, male |
| BMI *(backup RQ)* | Body mass index (primary exposure for the backup RQ) | Continuous, kg/m² |

3.3 Additional Variables of Interest (including potential confounders)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Age | Age of the participant at the time of screening | Integer, years (ages 80+ recorded as 80) |
| PhysActive | Whether the participant does moderate- or vigorous-intensity sports, fitness, or recreational activities | Factor: No, Yes |
| Poverty | Ratio of family income to the federal poverty guidelines; smaller values indicate more poverty | Continuous, 0--5 (values above 5 coded as 5) |
| Race1 | Self-reported race/ethnicity | Factor: Black, Hispanic, Mexican, White, Other |
| Education | Highest level of education completed | Factor: 8th Grade, 9 - 11th Grade, High School, Some College, College Grad |
| Smoke100 | Whether the participant has smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime | Factor: No, Yes |

#### 4 Statistical Analysis Plan

4.1 Exploratory Data Analysis

We will first examine the structure of the NHANES dataset and focus on adult participants aged 20 and older. For the primary research question, we will summarize the distribution of BMI using a histogram and report descriptive statistics, including the mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, minimum, and maximum.

To explore the relationship between sleep duration and BMI, we will calculate and plot mean BMI across reported sleep durations separately for men and women. Differences in these descriptive patterns may suggest potential effect modification by gender, which will be evaluated in the subsequent regression analysis. We will also present a "Table 2" summarizing selected participant characteristics by gender, including age, BMI, sleep duration, physical activity, and diabetes prevalence.

For the backup research question, we will report the proportion of participants with a self-reported diabetes diagnosis and compare BMI distributions between participants with and without diabetes using side-by-side boxplots grouped by gender.

4.2 Statistical Model

**Primary RQ (multiple linear regression):**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{BMI}_i = \; & \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Sleep}^c_i + \beta_2 \text{Male}_i + \beta_3 (\text{Sleep}^c_i \times \text{Male}_i) \\
& + \beta_4 \text{Black}_i + \beta_5 \text{Hispanic}_i + \beta_6 \text{Mexican}_i + \beta_7 \text{OtherRace}_i \\
& + \beta_8 \text{Edu911}_i + \beta_9 \text{HighSchool}_i + \beta_{10} \text{SomeCollege}_i + \beta_{11} \text{CollegeGrad}_i \\
& + \beta_{12} \text{Age}^c_i + \beta_{13} \text{PhysActive}_i + \beta_{14} \text{Poverty}_i + \beta_{15} \text{Smoke100}_i + \varepsilon_i, \\
& \varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2), \quad i = 1, \dots, n
\end{aligned}$$

where:

- $\text{BMI}_i$ is the body mass index (kg/m²) of participant $i$.
- $\text{Sleep}^c_i$ is hours of sleep per night centered at 7 hours ($\text{Sleep}_i - 7$).
- $\text{Age}^c_i$ is age in years centered at 50 ($\text{Age}_i - 50$).
- $\text{Male}_i$ = 1 if participant $i$ is male, 0 if female (reference).
- $\beta_0$ is the expected BMI for a female, White participant with an 8th-grade education who is 50 years old, sleeps 7 hours, is not physically active, has not smoked 100 cigarettes, and has a poverty ratio of 0. Because a poverty ratio of 0 (no family income) is rare, $\beta_0$ is not directly interpretable on its own.
- $\beta_1$ is the expected change in BMI for each additional hour of sleep among women, holding all other variables constant.
- $\beta_2$ is the expected difference in BMI between men and women who sleep 7 hours, holding all other variables constant.
- $\beta_3$ is the difference in the sleep--BMI slope between men and women; the slope for men is $\beta_1 + \beta_3$.
- $\beta_4$--$\beta_7$ are indicators for race/ethnicity (reference: White).
- $\beta_8$--$\beta_{11}$ are indicators for education level (reference: 8th Grade).
- $\beta_{12}$--$\beta_{15}$ are the coefficients for centered age (years), physical activity (1 = Yes), poverty ratio, and smoking history (1 = smoked at least 100 cigarettes).
- $\varepsilon_i$ is the random error, assumed independent and normally distributed with mean 0 and constant variance $\sigma^2$.

**Backup RQ (logistic regression):**

$$\begin{aligned}
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right) = \; & \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{BMI}^c_i + \beta_2 \text{Male}_i + \beta_3 (\text{BMI}^c_i \times \text{Male}_i) \\
& + \beta_4 \text{Age}^c_i + \dots + \beta_{15} \text{PhysActive}_i
\end{aligned}$$

where $Y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i)$, $p_i = P(\text{Diabetes}_i = \text{Yes})$, and $\text{BMI}^c_i$ is BMI centered at 25 kg/m² (the threshold for overweight), so that $e^{\beta_2}$ is the odds ratio of diabetes for men versus women with a BMI of 25. The covariates and reference groups are the same as in the primary model. Exponentiated coefficients are interpreted as odds ratios; for example, $e^{\beta_1}$ is the multiplicative change in the odds of diabetes for each 1 kg/m² increase in BMI among women.

4.2 Rationale for the statistical model

We will use multiple linear regression to examine the association between sleep duration and BMI, a continuous outcome. For the backup question, we will use logistic regression because diabetes diagnosis is binary (Yes/No); a linear model could produce predicted probabilities outside \[0, 1\], so we instead model the log-odds of diabetes through the logit link. This model allows us to estimate how the odds of diabetes vary with BMI while adjusting for the other variables.

Each model will include an interaction between the primary exposure and gender to assess whether the association differs between men and women. We will center sleep duration at 7 hours so that the gender coefficient in the primary model compares men and women who report 7 hours of sleep. In the backup model, centering BMI at 25 kg/m² makes the gender coefficient a comparison at the overweight threshold. Age will be centered at 50 years in both models.

We will adjust for age, race/ethnicity, education, poverty ratio, physical activity, and smoking history because these variables may be associated with both the exposure and the outcome. These adjustments are intended to account for potential confounding.

4.3 Model Assumptions

For the multiple linear regression model, we assume (1) **linearity**: the relationship between each continuous predictor and the expected BMI is linear; (2) **independence**: observations are independent of one another; (3) **normality**: the errors are normally distributed; and (4) **equal variance (homoscedasticity)**: the errors have constant variance across all fitted values.

For the logistic regression model, we assume (1) **linearity in the log-odds**: each continuous predictor has a linear relationship with the log-odds of diabetes; and (2) **independence** of observations. Normality and equal variance of errors are not required, since the outcome follows a Bernoulli distribution whose variance is determined by its mean.

**4.4 Model Assessment**

**Linear regression.**

We will plot residuals against fitted values and each continuous predictor (sleep duration, age, and poverty ratio) to check for curvature or other systematic patterns. The residuals-versus-fitted plot will also help us assess whether the residual spread changes across fitted values. We will use a normal Q-Q plot of standardized residuals to assess departures from normality. If the diagnostics suggest that a transformation may help, we will fit a model with log-transformed BMI and compare its diagnostics with those of the original model.

We will assess the independence assumption using the sampling design and data preparation steps. Removing duplicate participant IDs prevents repeated records for the same person, although this step alone does not establish independence.

We will check variance inflation factors (VIF) for multicollinearity. Values above 5 will prompt us to examine which predictors overlap; values above 10 will prompt a closer review of whether the model can distinguish their associations with BMI. We will examine the residuals-versus-leverage plot and Cook's distance for influential observations. Cook's distance values above 0.5 will be flagged for inspection, with particular attention to values above 1. We will check flagged records for data errors and compare estimates with and without them, rather than remove them solely because they exceed a threshold.

We will report adjusted R² and use a nested F test to compare models with and without the sleep × gender interaction.

**Logistic regression.**

We will use partial residual plots to assess whether BMI, age, and poverty ratio have approximately linear relationships with the log-odds of diabetes. We will assess independence and multicollinearity as described above. An influence plot showing hat values, studentized residuals, and Cook's distance will help identify observations for further inspection. We will compare estimates with and without influential observations to see whether the conclusions depend on a small number of participants.

We will use the Hosmer--Lemeshow test as one check of model fit. Because its result can depend on sample size and how predicted probabilities are grouped, we will consider it alongside the other diagnostics. We will use a likelihood ratio test to assess the BMI × gender interaction and report AIC for models with and without that term.

#### Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
library(NHANES)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

```{r}
data("NHANES")

# Restrict to adults aged 20+ and retain one record per ID
nhanes_eda <- NHANES %>%
  filter(Age >= 20) %>%
  distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Snapshot of variables relevant to our research questions
nhanes_eda %>%
  select(
    BMI, SleepHrsNight, Gender, Age,
    PhysActive, Poverty, Race1,
    Education, Smoke100, Diabetes
  ) %>%
  glimpse(width = 55)
```

```{r}
bmi_summary <- nhanes_eda %>%
  summarise(
    N = sum(!is.na(BMI)),
    Mean = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR = IQR(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min = min(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max = max(BMI, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

knitr::kable(
  bmi_summary,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Descriptive Statistics of BMI Among U.S. Adults"
)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(nhanes_eda, aes(x = BMI)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 2,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of BMI Among U.S. Adults",
    x = "Body Mass Index (kg/m²)",
    y = "Number of Participants"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Among the 4,654 adult participants, 4,609 had non-missing BMI measurements. The mean BMI was 28.90 kg/m² (SD = 6.81), while the median was 27.80 kg/m² (IQR = 8.02). The BMI distribution was right-skewed, with a small number of participants having substantially higher BMI values.\
\

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center

sleep_summary <- nhanes_eda %>%
  filter(!is.na(SleepHrsNight), !is.na(BMI)) %>%
  group_by(Gender, SleepHrsNight) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_BMI = mean(BMI),
    N = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  sleep_summary,
  aes(
    x = SleepHrsNight,
    y = Mean_BMI,
    color = Gender,
    group = Gender
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean BMI by Sleep Duration and Gender",
    x = "Usual Sleep Duration on Weeknights (hours)",
    y = "Mean Body Mass Index (kg/m²)",
    color = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Mean BMI varies across reported sleep durations for both genders. The observed patterns differ between men and women, suggesting that gender may modify the association between sleep duration and BMI. However, estimates at extreme sleep durations may be unstable because of smaller group sizes. These descriptive patterns do not establish a statistically significant interaction.

```{r}
table1 <- nhanes_eda %>%
  group_by(Gender) %>%
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean_Age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_BMI = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_BMI = sd(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Sleep = mean(SleepHrsNight, na.rm = TRUE),
    Physically_Active_Pct = 100 * mean(
      PhysActive == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    Diabetes_Pct = 100 * mean(
      Diabetes == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  table1,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Gender", "N", "Mean Age", "Mean BMI",
    "BMI SD", "Mean Sleep", "Active (%)", "Diabetes (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Selected Participant Characteristics by Gender"
)
```

Table 2 summarizes selected participant characteristics by gender. Female participants had a slightly higher mean BMI (29.16 vs. 28.63 kg/m²) and reported slightly longer sleep duration (6.93 vs. 6.80 hours) than male participants. Men reported higher levels of physical activity (53.94% vs. 47.75%) and a slightly higher prevalence of diagnosed diabetes (12.40% vs. 11.06%).\
\

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(
  nhanes_eda %>% filter(!is.na(Diabetes), !is.na(BMI)),
  aes(x = Diabetes, y = BMI, fill = Gender)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "BMI by Diabetes Diagnosis and Gender",
    x = "Reported Diabetes Diagnosis",
    y = "Body Mass Index (kg/m²)",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The boxplots compare BMI distributions between participants with and without a reported diabetes diagnosis, separately by gender. This descriptive comparison provides an initial view of the relationship between BMI and diabetes status. Any observed differences will require further assessment through the proposed logistic regression model.

### Dataset Option 2

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Project Title:** Flight Departure Delays at Raleigh–Durham International Airport: Does Departure Time Matter?

**Data citation:** U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics. (2026). *Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance (1987–present): July and August 2026* \[Data set\]. TranStats. https://www.transtats.bts.gov/DL_SelectFields.aspx?gnoyr_VQ=FGJ

**Direct data files:**

- July 2026: https://transtats.bts.gov/PREZIP/On_Time_Reporting_Carrier_On_Time_Performance_1987_present_2026_7.zip
- August 2026: https://transtats.bts.gov/PREZIP/On_Time_Reporting_Carrier_On_Time_Performance_1987_present_2026_8.zip

**Original data collection date:** July 1–August 31, 2026 (the dates of the reported flight operations). The monthly records were released after the flights took place.

**Data pull date:** Nov. 5th, 2026

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1 Research Question

**Primary RQ:** Among domestic flights departing from Raleigh–Durham International Airport (RDU) in July and August 2026, is the scheduled departure period (morning, afternoon, or evening) associated with the odds of leaving at least 15 minutes late, after adjusting for airline, flight distance, day of week, and month? Does this association differ by airline?

**Backup RQ:** Among domestic flights departing from RDU that reach their destination without being diverted, is flight distance associated with the odds of arriving at least 15 minutes late, after adjusting for airline, departure period, day of week, and month? Does this association differ by departure period?

#### 2 Study Population

The observation unit is one scheduled, nonstop domestic flight departing from Raleigh–Durham International Airport (RDU). The Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), part of the U.S. Department of Transportation, collects monthly on-time performance data submitted by reporting airlines. The data include scheduled and actual flight times, airlines, airports, delays, cancellations, and flight distance. These are operational records, not a random survey of passengers or flights from every airline worldwide.

We plan to use the July and August 2026 files, which are the two most recent complete months available at the time of this proposal. We will keep flights with RDU as the origin airport. For our primary analysis of departure delays, we will include flights that operated and have a recorded departure delay indicator. We will compare flights scheduled in the morning (5:00–11:59 a.m.), afternoon (12:00–5:59 p.m.), and evening (6:00–11:59 p.m.). Flights scheduled between midnight and 4:59 a.m. will not be part of this comparison because they are outside these three study periods. We will report how many flights are excluded for each reason.

We will first check the number of RDU flights, the available variables, and missing values using the EDA below. The original monthly BTS files have far more than the required ten variables and contain both numeric and categorical information. We will verify that the RDU subset meets the minimum of 300 observations before finalizing our proposal. We will not fit statistical models at this stage.

#### 3 Outcomes, Exposures, and Additional Variables of Interest

##### 3.1 Primary Outcome(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| `DepDel15` | Whether the flight departed at least 15 minutes after its scheduled departure time | Binary: 1 = delayed by 15 minutes or more; 0 = not delayed by 15 minutes |
| `ArrDel15` *(backup RQ)* | Whether the flight arrived at least 15 minutes late | Binary: 1 = delayed by 15 minutes or more; 0 = not delayed by 15 minutes |

##### 3.2 Primary Independent Variable(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| `CRSDepTime` | Scheduled departure time, used to create a departure-period variable | Local time in HHMM format; morning = 05:00–11:59; afternoon = 12:00–17:59; evening = 18:00–23:59. Morning is the reference period. |
| `Reporting_Airline` | Operating airline, used as a possible effect modifier | Categorical airline code; one airline will be the reference group. We will check group sizes before selecting the reference. |
| `Distance` *(backup RQ)* | Nonstop distance between the origin and destination airports | Continuous, miles; we plan to express distance in units of 100 miles |

##### 3.3 Additional Variables of Interest (including potential confounders)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| `Distance` | Distance flown, used to adjust for route length in the primary model | Continuous, miles; divided by 100 for interpretation |
| `DayOfWeek` | Day of the week when the flight was scheduled | Categorical: 1 = Monday through 7 = Sunday |
| `Month` | Month of the scheduled flight | Categorical: 7 = July; 8 = August |
| `Dest` | Destination airport | Categorical three-letter airport code; used in descriptive checks and possibly sensitivity analyses |
| `Cancelled` | Whether the flight was canceled | Binary: 1 = canceled; 0 = not canceled; canceled flights do not have an observed departure delay |
| `Diverted` | Whether the flight was diverted | Binary: 1 = diverted; 0 = not diverted; used to define the backup arrival-delay sample |
| `DepDelay` | Difference between actual and scheduled departure times | Continuous, minutes; negative values mean early departure |
| `ArrDelay` | Difference between actual and scheduled arrival times | Continuous, minutes; may be missing for canceled or diverted flights |
| `FlightDate` | Calendar date of the flight | Date; useful for checking daily patterns and possible dependence among flights |
| `CRSElapsedTime` | Scheduled length of the flight | Continuous, minutes; available for descriptive checks |

#### 4 Statistical Analysis Plan

##### 4.1 Exploratory Data Analysis

We will first use `glimpse()` to check the structure of the data. We will count the number of flights departing from RDU, look for missing values, and report how many flights were canceled or scheduled outside our three departure periods. This will help us understand which flights can be included in the departure-delay analysis.

Our main outcome is binary. We will report the overall number and percentage of flights that departed at least 15 minutes late, using a summary table and a bar chart. We will then calculate delay rates for morning, afternoon, and evening flights. A second plot will compare these three periods. We will also compare departure-delay rates by airline and departure period to look for possible differences between airlines. We will show the number of flights in each group so that small groups are easy to identify.

For additional context, we will report the mean flight distance and summarize the number of eligible flights across scheduled departure periods. We will also examine differences in departure-delay rates across the five most frequent reporting airlines. All EDA graphs will be made in R. The plots will describe the data only; they will not test our research questions or establish causation.

##### 4.2 Statistical Model

**Primary RQ (multiple logistic regression).** Let $Y_i=1$ if flight $i$ departed at least 15 minutes late, and $Y_i=0$ otherwise. We will model $Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i)$, where $p_i=P(Y_i=1)$. We plan to fit:

$$\begin{aligned}
\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
={}& \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathrm{Afternoon}_i + \beta_2\mathrm{Evening}_i\\
&+\sum_{c=1}^{C-1}\gamma_c\mathrm{Airline}_{ic}\\
&+\sum_{c=1}^{C-1}\delta_{Ac}\big(\mathrm{Afternoon}_i\times\mathrm{Airline}_{ic}\big)\\
&+\sum_{c=1}^{C-1}\delta_{Ec}\big(\mathrm{Evening}_i\times\mathrm{Airline}_{ic}\big)\\
&+\beta_3\mathrm{Distance100}_i + \beta_4\mathrm{August}_i\\
&+\sum_{d=2}^{7}\theta_d\mathrm{Day}_{id}.
\end{aligned}$$

where:

- $\mathrm{Afternoon}_i$ and $\mathrm{Evening}_i$ equal 1 when flight $i$ is scheduled in that period, and 0 otherwise. Morning is the reference period.
- $\mathrm{Airline}_{ic}$ is an indicator for operating airline $c$, with one airline as the reference. $C$ is the number of airline groups kept in the model.
- $\delta_{Ac}$ and $\delta_{Ec}$ are interaction coefficients. They tell us whether the association between departure period and delays differs by airline.
- $\mathrm{Distance100}_i$ is the scheduled nonstop distance in hundreds of miles.
- $\mathrm{August}_i$ is 1 for August and 0 for July.
- $\mathrm{Day}_{id}$ indicates the day of week, with Monday as the reference.

For the reference airline, $e^{\beta_1}$ compares the odds of a delay for afternoon versus morning flights, holding the other variables constant. Similarly, $e^{\beta_2}$ compares evening with morning. For another airline $c$, the corresponding odds ratio for evening versus morning is $e^{\beta_2+\delta_{Ec}}$. We will not interpret these as causal effects.

**Backup RQ (logistic regression).** We would model the chance of arriving at least 15 minutes late among flights with an observed arrival-delay indicator. The main predictor would be distance in hundreds of miles, with an interaction between distance and departure period, adjusting for airline, day of week, and month.

##### 4.2 Rationale for the Statistical Model

We chose logistic regression because the main outcome has two categories: a flight either departed at least 15 minutes late or it did not. Logistic regression models the log-odds of a delay and gives predicted probabilities between 0 and 1. This makes it more suitable than a linear regression for a binary outcome.

We will include airline, flight distance, day of week, and month because flight schedules and operating conditions differ across these groups. We will include an interaction between departure period and airline to see whether the morning-to-evening pattern is the same for all airlines. Before fitting the final model, we will check whether each airline has enough flights in the three periods. If some groups have very few flights, we may combine small airline groups and explain that choice in the final report.

##### 4.3 Model Assumptions

We assume (1) **a binary outcome**: each observed flight is classified as delayed or not delayed; (2) **linearity in the log-odds for continuous predictors**: flight distance has an approximately linear relationship with the log-odds of departure delay; (3) **no perfect separation**: no predictor group perfectly predicts the outcome; and (4) **limited dependence among observations**: flights are recorded individually, but flights from the same airline or on the same date may share operating conditions. We will also assess collinearity among predictors. Logistic regression does not require normally distributed errors or equal error variance.

Because these are observational data, unmeasured factors such as weather, airport congestion, arriving aircraft, crew availability, or flight-specific problems may affect the results. Also, the departure-delay model only covers operated flights with an observed delay indicator; canceled flights will be described separately rather than treated as on-time flights.

##### 4.4 Model Assessment

After the proposal stage, we will examine the number of observations and delays in each airline-by-period group. We will check for sparse groups and possible separation. We will assess whether flight distance is approximately linear on the log-odds scale, using an appropriate diagnostic plot or a more flexible functional form if needed. We will also examine multicollinearity and influential observations.

We will compare a model with the departure-period-by-airline interaction to a model without it using a likelihood ratio test, and we will consider AIC and overall model fit. We will review predicted probabilities and calibration rather than rely only on a classification accuracy number. Because several flights may be affected by the same day's conditions, we will consider a sensitivity analysis that accounts for clustering by flight date.

In the final report, we will present the exponentiated model coefficients (odds ratios), their 95% confidence intervals, standard errors with the scale clearly stated, and p-values. We will also explain the limitations of studying only one airport and two summer months. We will not fit any models for this proposal.

#### Exploratory Data Analysis

*The following R chunks load the official July and August 2026 monthly files, keep flights departing RDU, and produce descriptive tables and figures. No statistical models are fitted. This code needs internet access on its first run and the R packages listed below.*

```{r}
#| label: setup-rdu-data
#| results: hide
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(scales)

# Download data only once, then use local cached ZIP files.
data_dir <- file.path("data", "bts_2026")
dir.create(data_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

fields_needed <- c(
  "Year", "Month", "DayofMonth", "DayOfWeek", "FlightDate",
  "Reporting_Airline", "Flight_Number_Reporting_Airline",
  "Origin", "Dest", "CRSDepTime", "DepTime", "DepDelay",
  "DepDel15", "Cancelled", "Diverted", "Distance",
  "CRSElapsedTime", "ArrDel15", "ArrDelay"
)

read_rdu_month <- function(month_number) {
  file_name <- paste0(
    "On_Time_Reporting_Carrier_On_Time_Performance_1987_present_2026_",
    month_number, ".zip"
  )
  zip_path <- file.path(data_dir, file_name)
  url <- paste0("https://transtats.bts.gov/PREZIP/", file_name)

  if (!file.exists(zip_path)) {
    download.file(url, destfile = zip_path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }

  zip_contents <- unzip(zip_path, list = TRUE)$Name
  csv_files <- zip_contents[grepl("\\.csv$", zip_contents, ignore.case = TRUE)]
  if (length(csv_files) < 1) {
    stop("No CSV found in BTS ZIP for month ", month_number)
  }

  # Work with one month's data at a time to keep memory use lower.
  extract_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), paste0("bts_month_", month_number))
  dir.create(extract_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  csv_path <- unzip(zip_path, files = csv_files[1], exdir = extract_dir)[1]
  
  # Check that the required columns exist
  actual_fields <- names(
    data.table::fread(csv_path, nrows = 0)
  )
  
  missing_fields <- setdiff(fields_needed, actual_fields)
  
  if (length(missing_fields) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Missing BTS columns: ",
      paste(missing_fields, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }
  
  flight_data <- data.table::fread(
    csv_path, select = fields_needed,
    na.strings = c("", "NA"), showProgress = FALSE
  )
  unlink(extract_dir, recursive = TRUE)

  as_tibble(flight_data) %>%
    filter(Origin == "RDU")
}

rdu_all <- bind_rows(lapply(c(7, 8), read_rdu_month))

if (nrow(rdu_all) < 300) {
  stop("The RDU subset has fewer than 300 records; please review the source files.")
}

rdu_eda <- rdu_all %>%
  mutate(
    departure_hour = floor(as.numeric(CRSDepTime) / 100),
    departure_period = case_when(
      between(departure_hour, 5, 11) ~ "Morning",
      between(departure_hour, 12, 17) ~ "Afternoon",
      between(departure_hour, 18, 23) ~ "Evening",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    departure_period = factor(
      departure_period, levels = c("Morning", "Afternoon", "Evening")
    )
  )

rdu_delay <- rdu_eda %>%
  filter(Cancelled == 0,
         !is.na(DepDel15),
         !is.na(departure_period)) %>%
  mutate(delayed_15 = as.integer(DepDel15))

if (nrow(rdu_delay) < 300) {
  stop("The eligible RDU delay sample has fewer than 300 flights.")
}
# Check the final sample
cat("Total RDU flights:", nrow(rdu_all), "\n")
cat("Eligible flights:", nrow(rdu_delay), "\n")
cat("Number of variables:", ncol(rdu_all), "\n")

# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(
  rdu_delay[, c(
    "DepDel15",
    "CRSDepTime",
    "Reporting_Airline",
    "Distance",
    "DayOfWeek",
    "Month"
  )]
))

# Check airline and departure-period groups
rdu_delay %>%
  count(Reporting_Airline, departure_period) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rdu-delay-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Departure-delay summary for eligible RDU flights"
delay_overview <- rdu_delay %>%
  summarise(
    `Flights included` = n(),
    `Flights delayed 15+ minutes` = sum(delayed_15 == 1),
    `Delayed flights (%)` = 100 * mean(delayed_15 == 1),
    `Median departure delay (minutes)` = median(DepDelay, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Mean flight distance (miles)` = mean(Distance, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
knitr::kable(delay_overview, digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rdu-delay-outcome
#| fig-cap: "Departure-delay status among eligible flights from RDU, July–August 2026"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-align: center

rdu_delay %>%
  mutate(`Departure status` = if_else(
    delayed_15 == 1, "Delayed 15+ min", "Not delayed 15+ min"
  )) %>%
  count(`Departure status`) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Departure status`, y = n, fill = `Departure status`)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of flights") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rdu-time-period
#| tbl-cap: "Departure delays by scheduled time of day at RDU"
period_summary <- rdu_delay %>%
  group_by(departure_period) %>%
  summarise(
    `Number of flights` = n(),
    `Delayed flights` = sum(delayed_15 == 1),
    `Delay rate (%)` = 100 * mean(delayed_15 == 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

period_display <- period_summary %>%
  rename(`Scheduled departure period` = departure_period)
knitr::kable(period_display, digits = 1,
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rdu-period
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of flights departing 15 or more minutes late, by scheduled departure period"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(period_summary,
       aes(x = departure_period, y = `Delay rate (%)`)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(`Delay rate (%)`, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.35, size = 3.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled departure period", y = "Flights delayed 15+ minutes (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rdu-airlines
#| fig-cap: "Departure-delay rates by time of day for the five most frequent reporting airlines at RDU"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-align: center

# Display the five most common operating airlines to keep the plot readable.
top_airlines <- rdu_delay %>%
  count(Reporting_Airline, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(Reporting_Airline)

airline_period <- rdu_delay %>%
  filter(Reporting_Airline %in% top_airlines) %>%
  group_by(Reporting_Airline, departure_period) %>%
  summarise(
    `Flights` = n(),
    `Delay rate (%)` = 100 * mean(delayed_15 == 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(airline_period,
       aes(x = departure_period, y = `Delay rate (%)`,
           color = Reporting_Airline, group = Reporting_Airline)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled departure period",
       y = "Flights delayed 15+ minutes (%)",
       color = "Operating airline") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Among the 9,120 eligible RDU flights, approximately 27.2% departed at least 15 minutes late. The observed delay rate increased from 14.0% in the morning to 35.7% in the afternoon and 47.4% in the evening. Delay patterns also varied across airlines. These descriptive findings suggest that departure period and airline may be associated with delay risk, but further statistical modeling is needed to evaluate these relationships.\
